chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள்), not tied to a shrine: most confess the poet's bondage to courtesans and union with them and ask for Murugan's feet or teaching; others set out the body's frailty, a list of sinners bound for hell, the poet's past as a court poet of women's bodies, and a satire on the boasts of the Kali age turned into the poet's own modesty; the praise draws on the Ramayana, the Bharata war, Prahlada, Siva burning Kama and Murugan teaching Siva.
structure_note: Courtesans and union: 1142, 1144, 1145, 1147, 1148, 1151, 1152, 1153, 1154, 1156. 1143 and 1149 ask for the knowledge beyond the body and the sects; 1146 is a catalogue of sinners with a praise sung almost wholly in drum syllables; 1150 is a long self-accusation; 1155 is satire and modesty. Vishnu's avatars fill much of the praise (Ramayana in 1144, 1147, 1151, 1153; Bharata war in 1144; Gajendra in 1142; Prahlada in 1150).

1142.reading: The poet confesses that in this ruined, swaying hut of flesh he has been a wastrel driven by infatuation, nursing endless desire, quarrelling through the town, and standing like a dog in the power of honey-tongued courtesans, and asks when the day will come that Murugan grants the feet that devotees adorn with kadamba flowers. The praise names Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent, churned the sea with Meru, herded cattle and hurled the discus to cut down the crocodile when the elephant cried out, Murugan as his sister's treasure, who fell at the feet of the hunter girl in the millet field, and the lord who shattered the seven mountains and stirred the seven seas.
1142.nuance: பரத்தையர்க்கு ஒரு நாய்போலவே அவர் வசத்தில் நிற்பது: the courtesans are named by the Tamil word, and the poet's image for himself is a dog. சிறுப்பிள்ளைத்தனம், childishness, sums up the life. The elephant and crocodile are the Gajendra story (வாய் நாகம் ஓலமிட ... கர வினைத் தறித்தவர்).

1143.reading: The poet calls the body a raw clay pot with nine openings, soaked in two kinds of deed and disease, and asks that, not falling into the path of fools who never think how to reach the high state but sink in the sea of craving, he be taught one day from Murugan's Tamil-knowing mouth the dawning light of knowledge beyond the thirty-six, in which the three qualities and the seal of 'I' are destroyed. The praise names Siva who danced against Kali and asked to be told, and Murugan who whispered into his right ear that this was the supreme space of the bliss of consciousness, and Indra's son-in-law who killed Sura with the vel.
1143.nuance: முப்பதின் அறுபதின் மேலாம் may count the thirty-six tattvas and what lies beyond them, and நான் ஆ என வரு முத்திரை is the stamp of the ego; both readings depend on how the syllables split. The guru story has a new detail: the teaching is given into Siva's right ear (தெக்ஷண செவி), and what is taught is சிற்சுக பரவெளி, the space of conscious bliss, not Om by name.

1144.reading: The poet describes courtesans whose dark eyes, like Death's messengers, warriors' swords and the vel, take young men's lives for Kama's kingdom, how he melted in their arts until the wealth in his hand was gone, and how they then said 'no shame? go, go now, mother, call the others'; he asks that his love for these deceivers end. The praise names Krishna, charioteer of Dharma, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva against the king of Hastinapura, and Rama who felled Ravana's ten heads and twenty arms with one arrow, as Murugan's uncle.
1144.nuance: The dismissal is given in the courtesans' own words (வெட்கமிலை நட ஏகும் ஏகும் இனி மற்றவரை அழையும் மாதரே), so the turn comes exactly when the money is gone (பொருளான ஆகும் வரை). படிறிகள், deceivers, is the poet's last word for them.

1145.reading: The poet describes union, loosened hair, pressed breasts, reddened eyes, lips like the red indragopa insect, coos like the cuckoo and the dove, nail marks, and asks when he will leave this hut of a body, worn out in that pit, and reach Murugan's lotus feet. The praise tells how the sea burned and the Krauncha hill was split, how Indra regained his place and Devayanai her bridegroom, and names Murugan with the rooster banner, wearing kadamba and loved by the hunter girl.
1145.nuance: குரம்பை, a hut, for the body, is the word that turns the scene: the poet asks to leave it (விட்டு அகன்று) for the feet. One line is garbled (see source issues).

1146.reading: The song lists sinners: those who do not pay the teacher who taught them, who wrong great ascetics, Brahmins who harm their own town, those who give nothing to the beggar, who are partial, who mock those who serve Siva and Vishnu, who have no single-minded meditation, who are steeped in lust; all of them, it says, will suffer in the seven hells. The praise is almost wholly drum syllables (தாதத, தூதுது, சாசச, டுட்டுடு ...) for Murugan's dance, praised by the learned.
1146.nuance: There is no first-person plea: the first half is a moral catalogue ending in ஏழ் நரகு உழல்வாரே. ஈசர் விஷ்ணுவை சேவை செய்வோர் protects the devotees of both Siva and Vishnu. Several items in the list (ஊசலிற் கனலாய் எரி காளையர், ஆர் தனக்கும் உதாசின தாரிகள்) are hard to construe, so the list is only roughly read.

1147.reading: The poet describes courtesans whose eyes reach their palm-leaf earrings, who trouble even ascetics learned in wisdom with the poison set in their eye-arrows, catch good wealth at their fragrant breasts and lead a man in with 'come', and asks that their illusion be ended and he be given the true akshara that was given to the gods. The praise tells how Nala threw mountains into the sea for Rama's bridge, Vibhishana received grace and the demons died, names Siva who destroyed Kama's body, and Murugan who fell in love in the millet field.
1147.nuance: ஞானம் ஓதி மிகுத்த தவத்தவர்க்கு இடர் ஓகை செலுத்தி: the women's eyes threaten even ascetics, a point the confession uses against itself. வானவருக்கு அருளுற்ற அக்ஷர வாய்மை may mean an imperishable truth or a sacred syllable; I cannot tell which.

1148.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes reach their earrings, their loosened cloth and hair, their lips and play, and asks whether one day the frenzy of ripe lust will subside and, knowing Murugan, he will reach the blissful state practised in the cage of silence and abide in grace. The praise tells how the northern mountains wailed, the earth rejoiced, Indra regained his city, the sea shrank and Sura's mango tree was torn up by the root, and names Murugan who embraced the daughter raised by the elephant.
1148.nuance: மவுன பஞ்சரம், the cage of silence, turns the image of a caged bird into the goal: the silence where knowing Murugan (உனை உணர்ந்து) brings bliss (சுக பதம்). The plea grows directly out of lust subsiding (காம பரவசம் தணிந்து).

1149.reading: The poet speaks of the One that the clamouring arts cannot point to and the warring sects cannot reach, the great light seen when birth and the two deeds end, which the Vedas melt toward and which is reached by letting go of everything, and confesses that, not knowing it, he is caught in the net of women's eyes, musk and brow-marks; he asks whether he must suffer. The praise names Murugan as the child with anklets whose feet the Vedas worship, nursed by the stars, born on the hundred-petalled lotus bed in the pond, who crushed Sura and the golden mountain, lord of the gods.
1149.nuance: The opening is a negative theology: ஏகம் is what the பதறிய சமயிகள் cannot reach and is found only by leaving all (முழுதையும் விட்டால் சேர்வது). The praise's pond and lotus (பாசடை, டாமரை, சததள அமளி) seem to describe the birth in the Saravana pool, though the pool is not named; one word is corrupt.

1150.reading: The poet accuses himself at length: he was a poet who sang women's bodies from foot to head, a lustful, angry rogue, a deceiver, unsettled, who argued for shastras in every sect without discipline, followed the five senses, took this passing life as lasting and was caught in the bonds of the bound soul; he asks to be guarded and brought to the flowered feet, having at least a little desire for the reality that destroys the qualities, deeds and maya. The praise names Siva who burned Kama with a look when he broke his yoga, Narasimha who came from the pillar for the child who said 'namo Narayana', and Murugan who freed Indra from fear and drove off Sura.
1150.nuance: பாதாதிகேசம் அளவும் பாடும் கவிஞனாய்த் திரிவேனை: the poet confesses the very genre of praising women limb by limb, which his own confessions resemble. ஆசாரவீன சமயம் தோறும் களவு சாத்திரம் ஓதி may mean he argued false doctrines in every sect; the phrase is uncertain, as is மூகம் தனிற் பிறந்து.

1151.reading: The poet describes women with eyes darker than a vel, drinking their lips, embracing them, nail marks and slipping cloth, and confesses that he sees no way to end it and no companion to help. The praise turns the same gaze on Valli, her anklets, peacock-feather dress, breasts and spear-like eyes that drove Murugan to longing until he joined her, and names Rama who killed Ravana, Siva who bent Meru as a bow, and Murugan as the servant-hero honoured by both.
1151.nuance: The second half describes Valli's body in the same terms as the courtesans' (கண்கள், தனங்கள், ஓதி), and has the Lord's mind tremble (மனம் பரதவிக்க), so the desire the poet cannot end is shown sanctified in Murugan's love. ஒன்றுகாணேன் twice, 'I see none', is the plea's whole force. Who is மாயான் whose mind is troubled (line 12) is not certain.

1152.reading: The poet runs through a woman's hair, brow, ears, eyes, nose, lips, teeth, breasts, gait, waist and feet, and asks that his heart not weaken at them, and that Murugan grant the meaning he told Agastya and the lotus feet that Hari and Brahma could not measure. The praise names the vel that killed the demons and restored the gods to their cities, and Murugan who embraced the hunter girl in the forest where the hunters wrest the tusks from elephant herds.
1152.nuance: அகத்தியனொடு உரைத்த பொருள் makes Murugan Agastya's teacher; the text gives the 'meaning', not Tamil by name. The catalogue of the woman's parts in -க்கும் is answered by the feet that cannot be measured (அளப்பரிய பதக்கமலம்).

1153.reading: The poet tells how, caught by peacock-like women's games in an unrighteous mind, he climbed on their flowered bed and drowned in a sea of passion, and asks that even he, a dog in their power, be raised. The praise tells the Ramayana: Rama going to the forest at his mother's word with Sita and Lakshmana, the golden deer Maricha, Khara and Dushana, the seven trees and Vali, Hanuman and the bridge, and the single arrow that felled Ravana's ten heads, with Murugan as his nephew.
1153.nuance: The poet calls himself கொடிய மனது அநியாய மாபாதகா போதி, a great sinner of crooked mind. The Ramayana is told in order and at unusual length, but as stock praise of the uncle. The word for the deer is corrupt (see source issues).

1154.reading: The poet describes union in doubled words, eyes rolling, waist bending, bangles crying out, lips drunk again and again, and how after a few days, his wealth and good name gone, everyone drove him off with 'chi, chi', and asks whether he must wander the world. The praise is a battle in doubled words, the sea drying, mountains shattering, Sura's strength failing and jackals and owls following, ending with the vel.
1154.nuance: The doubling (சுழலச் சுழல, குவியக் குவிய ...) runs through both halves, so the union and the war share one rhythm. கையிலுள பொருள்கெட்டு அருள்கெட்டு is the turn: money and grace go together.

1155.reading: The poet mocks the boasts of the age: cowards proclaim their valour, men of low birth claim high lineage and sit in the middle, those who feed no one call themselves Dharmaputra, the poor call themselves Kubera; this, he says, is the way of the Kali age, and he, without real knowledge, is no different, so this song is his apology to the assembly. The praise names Murugan who came to Kailas to end the gods' distress, freed Indra from prison and released Brahma, and took up the bow while vultures pecked at Sura's crown.
1155.nuance: அவையடக்க உரையீதே: the song names itself as the convention by which a poet abases himself before the learned. The satire turns on the poet in one line (நானும் வேறல அதற்குள் ஆகையால்). The opening of the praise (ஆனை வாசவன் உருத்ர ஈசன் மேல் வெயில் எறிக்க) I cannot construe with confidence.

1156.reading: The poet describes adorned women swaying through the street, their bangles, hair and anklets, and asks to be freed from their embraces and given Murugan's feet. The praise names the anklets on Murugan's own feet as he comes, the hunter girl of the champak field whose breasts he embraced, the son of Uma who shares Siva's body, and the lord who enters the hearts of loving devotees.
1156.nuance: The women's anklets (வண்சிலம்பு பொங்க) are answered by Murugan's (செஞ்சிலம்பு கிண்கிணி ... தண்டை), the same sound turned to the Lord's coming.

links.note: Both make the courtesan's love last as long as the man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out when the oil ends; in 1154 the wealth in his hand is gone and everyone drives him off with 'chi, chi'.

The Kural says smallness adorns itself in self-praise; 1155 gives the examples, the coward praising his valour and the miser calling himself Dharmaputra, and then applies the charge to the poet himself.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them; 1155 mocks men of base lineage (இழிகுலத்தர்) for claiming a high one, which treats birth-rank as real. The conflict holds if இழிகுலத்தர் is read literally as low caste rather than as a term of abuse for base men.
Both send to hell those who give nothing to the one who begs. Tirumular adds those who do not praise the Lord or tend groves; 1146 adds those who do not pay their teacher.
Both put in deep hell those who speak ill of the Lord's devotees. Tirumular means Siva's devotees; 1146 names the servants of both Siva and Vishnu (ஈசர் விஷ்ணுவை சேவைசெய்வோர்).

1143 calls the body a raw clay pot with eight openings and one (எட்டுடன் ஒரு தொளை ... பசு மட்கலம்) soaked in deeds and disease; Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot (கும்பம்) seeping from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்) that the fool praises for its skin. Naladiyar uses the pot to cure desire; the song uses it to ask for the knowledge beyond the tattvas.

1144's courtesans, once the wealth in his hand is gone, say 'no shame? go, go now, call the others' (வெட்கமிலை நட ஏகும் ஏகும் இனி மற்றவரை அழையும்). Naladiyar 373 says such women would bow and send away even red-eyed Mal if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன்று இல்லாரை ... விடுப்பர்). The song gives the dismissal in the women's own words.

Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in a corner of the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) has no home of its own. 1145 calls the body a hut (குரம்பை) worn out in the pit of union and asks when, leaving it (விட்டு அகன்று), he will reach Murugan's lotus feet. The song names the home the Kural's question leaves open.

1148 asks that, lust subsiding, he reach the blissful state practised in the cage of silence (மவுன பஞ்சரம் பயில் தரும் சுக பதம்) and abide in grace. Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come (மோனம் கைவந்தோர்க்கு) release too comes to hand. Both make silence the threshold of release.

1149 speaks of the One the clamouring arts cannot point to and the warring sects cannot reach (பதறிய சமயிகள் எட்டாப் பேரொளி), found only by letting go of everything. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him and he is not what the six sects hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). Both place the goal outside the sects; the song adds renunciation as the way, the Tirumanthiram clarity.

64 scorns those who sit singing a few poor poems (புன்கவி சில பாடி) about a lovesick girl and do not know to praise Senthil. 1150 confesses that he was himself such a poet, wandering as one who sang women's bodies from foot to head (பாதாதி கேசம் அளவும் பாடும் கவிஞனாய்த் திரிவேனை). The charge of the early song becomes the poet's own self-accusation.

1150 confesses he was a poet who sang women from foot to head (பாதாதிகேசம்); two songs later, 1152 runs through hair, brow, ears, eyes, lips, teeth, breasts, gait, waist and feet in one catalogue (குழற்கு ... அடிக்கும்) before asking that his heart not weaken. 1152 performs the genre 1150 names as a fault, and turns it into a plea.

1150 counts among his faults that he took this passing life as lasting (மாதேச வாழ்வை நிலையென்றே). Kural 331 calls exactly this, taking what does not last as lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்), the lowest kind of understanding. The song lists the Kural's verdict as one item in a confession.

1151 confesses he sees no way to end his passion and no companion to help (ஒழிக்க ஓர் வகை காணேன் உறுந்துணை ஒன்று காணேன்). Kural 1164's woman says the sea of love is there but no raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்), which commentators read as having no helper. Both name the lack of a helper out of desire; the song then finds it in Murugan, who himself longed for Valli.

1152 asks Murugan to grant the meaning he told Agastya (அகத்தியனொடு உரைத்த பொருள்); 598 asks for the honey-nectar of the virtuous Agastya's knowledge (சீல அகத்திய ஞான தேனமுது). Both ask for the teaching Murugan gave Agastya, 598 as escape from death and birth, 1152 as the cure for a heart weakened by a woman's body.

source_issues: Song 1145: garbled line 3 (....... ; ந்த்ரகோபம்), probably இந்த்ரகோபம், the red velvet insect.
Song 1149: corrupt று஡டொரு (line 16), probably ஆற்றூடொரு (஡ for ஊ).
Song 1153: corrupt மா஡ணச (line 16), probably மாரீச (Maricha); unflagged ஆரமுநல்முழ்கி (line 6), probably ஆரமும் உழ்கி or மூழ்கி.
